title: Gnocchi di Patate
subtitle: Classic Italian potato gnocchi
excerpt: Gnocchi di patate are soft, light potato dumplings made from floury potatoes, a small amount of flour, egg, and salt. The key is to use as little flour as possible while still getting dumplings that hold together. Too much flour produces dense, stodgy gnocchi. Good gnocchi are pillowy and delicate.
sourceNotes: Potato gnocchi have been made in northern and central Italy since the potato was established as a staple in the eighteenth century. The Veneto is considered the heartland of the tradition, with gnocchi appearing as the Thursday pasta of Venetian domestic cooking.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze shaped gnocchi on a floured tray, then bag. Cook from frozen in boiling salted water -- they are done when they float.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the batch and freeze half before cooking.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cook and use the same day. Uncooked gnocchi can rest on a floured tray for up to 1 hour before cooking.

content.text: The single most important rule in gnocchi making is to use floury potatoes (Maris Piper, King Edward, or Desir\u00e9e) and to dry them out as much as possible before mixing. Baking the potatoes rather than boiling them removes water efficiently. Rice the potato while still hot and spread it to cool and steam for a few minutes before adding flour. Every gram of excess water you remove from the potato means less flour needed -- and lighter, better gnocchi.

items.prepNote: large baking potatoes, washed but not peeled
plus extra for dusting -- use less if the dough comes together sooner

content.text: Preheat the oven to 200C. Pierce the {{potatoes-floury}} potatoes several times and bake directly on the oven rack for 50 to 60 minutes until completely soft. Cut in half and scoop out the flesh. Pass through a potato ricer immediately while hot. Spread the riced potato on a clean surface and leave to cool and steam for 5 minutes.

Make a well in the riced potato. Add {{eggs}} egg, {{salt-table}} salt, and two-thirds of the {{00-flour}} flour. Mix gently with your hands, adding more flour only until the dough just comes together and is no longer sticky. Do not overwork it.

Divide the dough into portions. Roll each into a rope about 2cm thick on a lightly floured surface. Cut into 2cm pieces. Roll each piece over the back of a fork or a gnocchi board to make ridges. Place on a floured tray.

Bring a large pan of well-salted water to a boil. Cook gnocchi in batches -- they are done when they float to the surface, after about 2 minutes. Lift with a slotted spoon straight into the sauce and toss to coat. Serve immediately.

items.symptom: The gnocchi are dense and heavy
items.cause: Too much flour, or the potato was not dried enough.
items.fix: Use the minimum flour needed to bring the dough together. Add it gradually -- a dough that seems slightly sticky is better than one that is over-floured. Always bake rather than boil the potatoes.

items.symptom: The gnocchi fall apart in the water
items.cause: Too little flour, or the dough was too wet.
items.fix: Test one gnocchi first. If it breaks up, knead in a little more flour and test again before cooking the rest.

content.text: Potato gnocchi are made across central and northern Italy. In Venice the tradition is to eat them on Thursday -- gnocch\u00ec de venterd\u00ec in Venetian dialect. In Rome they appear as gnocchi al giovedi (Thursday gnocchi), also a weekly habit. The Veneto, Friuli, and the Alpine foothills of Lombardy are the heartland of the tradition. These basic potato gnocchi are the base for many sauced versions.
